title: Where to Pitch When You Don’t Have a Warm Intro
summary: Where to Pitch When You Don’t Have a Warm Intro
body_markdown:
A warm introduction helps because someone supplies context before the investor opens your note. If you don't have an introduction, you still need to supply the context. The usual cold email tries to make up for the missing introduction by adding adjectives. That makes the reader do more work, at precisely the point where you are asking them to do less.


## Start with a route the investor chose


Look on the firm’s own site for a pitch form, an application, or a clear invitation to reach out.[Forum Ventures](https://lp.forumvc.com/pitch-us-form) has a pitch form.[Beta Boom](https://www.betaboom.com/investment-process) describes an intake form as the first step.[Sidecut](https://www.sidecut.vc/pitch) has a dedicated pitch page. They’re useful because they tell you where to put the information, and sometimes what the firm wants to know. Even an active form is not evidence the firm will invest in your stage or market; check that separately.


A firm intake, an accelerator application and a personal email are different requests. An accelerator may involve a location, cohort or terms you wouldn't accept in a regular financing. Don’t add a program to your list until you would actually consider the program. And don’t send the same pitch through every route you can find. If a firm tells founders which channel to use, start there.


## Put the buyer before the category


If you make bookkeeping software for two-location dental practices, lead with what happens to a dental practice on Friday afternoon. ‘We match insurer deposits to patient accounts for small dental groups’ tells the reader enough to picture a person at work. ‘We’re transforming finance with AI’ could describe dozens of companies, none of which the reader can remember.


Then offer one fact that would still be impressive without a deck. Numbers help when the unit and time window are clear. ‘In six pilot offices, five used it each week for the past month’ means something. So does ‘three offices sent us last quarter’s records and asked to switch.’ Use whichever fact you actually have. A tiny observation you can defend beats an impressive paragraph you can't.


## Ask for a small decision


After saying why you picked that firm, give the reader one next step. You can ask whether this fits the current fund or whether they would look at a short demo. If a form asks for a deck, give it one a stranger can read without you. Track the route, date and answer. If you follow up, send a development that makes the original note more useful, then move on if there’s still no fit.


A cold pitch works best when it resembles a useful piece of information someone was glad to get. The next time you write one, remove the words about how exciting the company is and see whether the note got stronger.
